title: The FAA's plan to fix air traffic? $875M worth of AI
content:
The Federal Aviation Administration has been struggling to manage an air traffic control shortage throughout the country. The reasons for the shortage are diverse, but the government has made it known that it’s on the lookout for innovative solutions to the problem.
One of those solutions appears to be an $875 million AI software program that is expected to help air traffic controllers manage their workflows and more safely navigate flight routes.
The Wall Street Journal reports that the FAA will soon launch SMART, which stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories — an automated software program designed to help streamline air traffic operations.
A one-page readout on the program describes SMART as “a cloud-based platform system that enhances existing FAA air traffic management systems.” It adds that the program uses AI to assess “airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions, and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur.”
SMART, the product of a firm called Air Space Intelligence, will cost the government that amount over a 12-year period, the outlet writes. The software will roll out in the Washington, D.C., metropolitan area first before expanding to other regions, it says.
Earlier this year, the FAA also announced a “bold, new” hiring plan that the agency said would “erase the longstanding staffing shortage,” and the government is separately engaged in a broad effort to modernize the nation’s aging air traffic systems.

report.summary: FAA plans to deploy SMART, an $875M AI platform from Air Space Intelligence over 12 years, to help air traffic controllers predict and prevent conflicts.
report.background: The FAA has struggled with a nationwide air traffic controller shortage driven by retirements, training bottlenecks, and pandemic-era disruptions. At the same time, U.S. air traffic systems are aging, and flight demand has rebounded, increasing pressure on controllers and infrastructure. The government has sought innovative fixes, including a new hiring plan and broader modernization efforts. AI is increasingly viewed as a way to augment human controllers rather than replace them, by forecasting traffic flows and flagging potential conflicts earlier. SMART, a cloud-based platform, reflects that shift: it will analyze schedules, weather, capacity, airspace conditions, and operational constraints. The $875 million, 12-year contract signals a major federal bet on AI-assisted aviation operations, starting in the Washington, D.C., region.
key_points: The FAA will soon launch SMART, or Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, a cloud-based AI program meant to enhance existing air traffic management systems. It assesses airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions, and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify conflicts before they happen.

SMART is built by Air Space Intelligence and will cost $875 million over a 12-year period, according to The Wall Street Journal. The rollout will begin in the Washington, D.C., metropolitan area before expanding to other regions, making it a phased federal deployment rather than an immediate nationwide switch.

The program directly targets the FAA’s controller shortage by streamlining workflows and helping controllers safely navigate flight routes. It is positioned as a decision-support tool, not a replacement for human controllers, and forms part of a wider government push to modernize aging air traffic systems.

Earlier this year, the FAA announced a hiring plan intended to erase its longstanding staffing shortage. SMART adds an AI layer to that effort, suggesting the agency is pursuing both workforce expansion and automation-assisted operations to address capacity and safety concerns.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the SMART contract validates large-scale government spending on AI in safety-critical infrastructure, potentially opening doors for aviation, logistics, and public-sector forecasting startups. Developers will need expertise in cloud platforms, real-time data integration, simulation, explainable AI, and human-in-the-loop design, because safety certification and controller trust are essential. For regular travelers, the payoff could be fewer delays, smoother routing, and safer operations, though benefits will depend on successful rollout and adoption. The high price tag also invites scrutiny over procurement, performance metrics, and whether AI can reliably handle rare, high-stakes airspace conflicts.
report.tools: To follow this space, watch FAA SMART and Air Space Intelligence. For hands-on exploration, try BlueSky ATC Simulator, an open-source air traffic control simulator; OpenSky Network and ADS-B Exchange for live flight data; and the Python library Traffic for ADS-B processing. General ML stacks like PyTorch or scikit-learn can prototype traffic-flow forecasting, while NASA airspace research tools offer broader ATM modeling context.
